title: China Upgrades VT-4 Tank Used by Pakistan With Anti-Drone Gun, Stronger Armour
excerpt: The upgraded export tank, believed to be designated the VT-4B, adds a 30mm remote weapon station aimed at FPV drones and an active protection system, and is set for display at the Zhuhai airshow next month, the SCMP reported.
body:
• China has developed an upgraded version of the VT-4 main battle tank - a key component of Pakistan's armoured fleet - with stronger armour, improved sensors and a larger weapon station, the South China Morning Post reported.
  • A 30mm remotely operated weapon station replaces the standard 12.7mm roof machine gun, intended to counter loitering munitions and first-person-view drones.
  • The variant, believed to be designated VT-4B, appears to carry an active protection system with radar panels giving 360-degree threat detection.
  • Pakistan's contract covers 679 VT-4s to be produced under licence as the Haider, according to SIPRI data; whether Islamabad will seek the upgraded variant is not yet clear.

China has upgraded the VT-4 main battle tank it builds for export, adding heavier armour, an anti-drone weapon station and an active protection system to a vehicle that forms a key part of the Pakistan Army's armoured fleet, according to a report by the South China Morning Post (SCMP). The new version, believed to be designated the VT-4B, is expected to be displayed at the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai from December 7 to 13, India Today reported.

"The armour has been substantially reinforced, with thicker explosive reactive armour across the front hull and sides, extending lower to protect the front section and parts of the running gear."

What has changed

The most visible change is on the roof: a 30mm remotely operated weapon station replaces the standard 12.7mm machine gun fitted on most Chinese tanks. According to the SCMP, the larger gun is meant to give the crew more firepower against loitering munitions and first-person-view (FPV) drones - the cheap aerial threats that have destroyed large numbers of tanks in recent wars - as well as infantry and anti-tank teams. The armour has been substantially reinforced, with thicker explosive reactive armour across the front hull and sides, extending lower to protect the front section and parts of the running gear. The upgraded tank also appears to be fitted with an active protection system, believed to be China's GL-6, with four phased-array radar panels mounted on the turret for 360-degree threat detection and two interceptor launchers near the rear of the turret. Some of the improvements borrow traits from technologies developed for China's newer domestic armour, including the Type 100 family and the upgraded Type 99B, the SCMP reported, although the VT-4B keeps the basic design of a third-generation main battle tank.

Pakistan's fleet, and the China link

The VT-4 is built by Norinco primarily for export and is in service with the armies of Pakistan, Thailand and Nigeria. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's (SIPRI) arms transfers data, Pakistan signed a contract to acquire 679 VT-4 tanks, to be assembled and produced under licence in Pakistan under the name Haider. SIPRI estimates that Pakistan's army, air force and navy operate around 80 per cent Chinese weapon systems. It is not immediately clear whether Pakistan will seek to acquire the upgraded VT-4B, or whether the upgrade package will be offered to existing export customers at all.

Why it matters for India

The VT-4 equips the Pakistan Army's modern strike formations, the armoured units that would face India in any conventional conflict on the western border. An upgrade aimed squarely at the drone threat reflects the lesson armies have drawn from recent conflicts: armour that cannot deal with FPV drones and loitering munitions does not survive on a modern battlefield. For Indian planners, the question the Zhuhai display will begin to answer is whether the VT-4B stays a showpiece or becomes the new standard for Pakistan's fleet - and on what timeline.

What happens next

The tank's public debut at Zhuhai next month will show the upgrade in full for the first time. Any Pakistani decision on the VT-4B would follow the pattern of the original programme - evaluation, then licence production at Heavy Industries Taxila - but no such move has been announced, and the extent of the upgrade offer to existing customers remains uncertain.
